scenarios.title: Recover the intended system root
scenarios.summary: Repair a boot entry whose filesystem identifier points to an archive instead of the operating system.
scenarios.objective: Use the Operations system UUID 31415926-5358-9793-2384-626433832795 with the supplied 7.0 kernel and matching initramfs. Request an initially read-only root and ordinary multi-user startup. Test the edited entry until all requested outcomes match.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Read the first blocked stage, compare it with the supplied image/root facts, edit the relevant line and test again.
steps: Inspect the supplied entry and image/root facts
Repair the relevant boot configuration
Test the full requested handoff
scenarios.explanation: The entry loads its kernel and initramfs, but the archive has no init program. The right repair changes the root=UUID= argument using the filesystem inventory; a different title cannot redirect the handoff.
hints: linux and initrd name supplied images relative to virtual $BOOT. title/version are descriptions, not path substitutions.
An existing image can have the wrong release or lack a required early-boot driver.
A valid handoff must still use the requested root, kernel release, initial mode and target.
scenarios.simplifications: Bounded Type #1 Linux boot-entry editing and hypothetical early-root handoff over supplied facts. Firmware/loader availability are preconditions. No GRUB installation/config generation, BLS discovery/order, Secure Boot, image parsing, initramfs generation, actual kernel/init/service execution, disk or host access. Only the disclosed literal keys and kernel options are supported.

Recovery also has an outcome requirement: a valid kernel and root can reach ordinary startup while still missing the requested rescue target or initial read-only mode. This is a combined configuration task, not a real rollback or reboot.

An existing image can have the wrong release or lack a required early-boot driver.
A valid handoff must still use the requested root, kernel release, initial mode and target.

scenarios.title: Choose a working fallback from a GRUB menu
scenarios.summary: Diagnose a failed upgrade and select the supplied ordinary fallback without damaging another boot path.
scenarios.objective: Select the supplied known-working 7.0 ordinary entry for system UUID 31415926-5358-9793-2384-626433832795; use an explicit default. Preserve all three supplied entries’ titles, image paths and kernel settings. A recovery target or repaired 7.1 upgrade is not the requested fallback.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Read the first blocked stage, compare it with the supplied image/root facts, edit the relevant line and test again.
steps: Inspect the menu choice and supplied image facts
Edit the relevant GRUB setting or entry
Test the selected handoff and preserve the other path
scenarios.explanation: The upgraded entry lacks an early storage driver. Selecting the intact previous entry reaches ordinary startup with the required 7.0 kernel; the recovery entry is bootable but requests a different target. IDs, positions and titles can express the same supported selection.
hints: Read Actual test result from Menu selection, then the first blocked image or handoff stage.
Positions start at 0; a short identifier written as --id=... or quoted title can identify the same supplied entry.
linux chooses an image; root=UUID= and systemd.unit= are kernel arguments. initrd must follow linux and match its release.
scenarios.simplifications: Bounded hand-authored flat GRUB2 menu subset over supplied virtual boot/image/filesystem facts. No GRUB execution, firmware, installation, generation, distribution templates, saved environment, submenus, device/search commands, expansion, real images or host files. Unknown syntax and missing-default fallback are explicitly unsupported; this is not advice to edit a distribution-generated grub.cfg.

initial.instructions: Select the supplied known-working 7.0 ordinary entry for system UUID 31415926-5358-9793-2384-626433832795; use an explicit default. Preserve all three supplied entries’ titles, image paths and kernel settings. A recovery target or repaired 7.1 upgrade is not the requested fallback.

example.instructions: Select the supplied working 7.0 ordinary-startup entry for system UUID 11223344-5566-7788-99aa-bbccddeeff00. Keep all three entries' supplied configuration. Use an explicit default and test the whole chosen path; do not repair the failed upgrade or substitute the recovery target.

scenarios.objective: Select and repair entry ID recovery for kernel 7.1 and system UUID 31415926-5358-9793-2384-626433832795. Use matching complete early-boot support, initial ro mode and systemd.unit=rescue.target. Preserve the supplied normal entry’s title, image paths and kernel settings; changing that entry cannot replace the recovery repair.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Read the first blocked stage, compare it with the supplied image/root facts, edit the relevant line and test again.

Edit the relevant GRUB setting or entry
Test the selected handoff and preserve the other path
scenarios.explanation: The recovery entry uses a mismatched early image and points to data rather than the operating system. Matching complete 7.1 early support plus the correct system UUID, initial ro mode and rescue request reaches the intended recovery handoff. Changing the intact normal entry is unnecessary.

scenarios.title: Make a GRUB choice survive regeneration
scenarios.summary: Edit persistent defaults, generate the virtual menu and verify the selected rollback path.
scenarios.objective: Generate a menu that selects the supplied 7.0 ordinary-startup entry for system UUID 31415926-5358-9793-2384-626433832795. Allow 8 seconds to choose another entry. Keep every supplied normal and recovery path bootable with initial root mode ro; normal entries should receive quiet and recovery entries should not. Test the menu generated from the current settings. Editing or filling settings alone is not a tested configuration.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Read the generated-menu status first. If it is outdated, generate again; otherwise inspect the failed entry or timer requirement, edit the relevant settings, generate and retry.
steps: Understand the persistent settings and supplied templates
Edit, generate and inspect the menu
Test all requested outcomes
scenarios.explanation: Settings and a generated menu are different saved artifacts. A zero-second timer hides the chance to choose recovery; the supplied rollback is selected by an existing ID, title or zero-based position. Only generating the edited settings changes the menu.
hints: Read Supplied menu templates to distinguish a normal entry from a recovery entry; the currently selected entry is a separate choice.
Generate menu uses the current settings. Inspect generated menu is read only and names its actual timeout and entries.
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX reaches both entry classes; GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT adds arguments only to normal entries. Later ro/rw values take precedence in this modeled kernel subset.
scenarios.simplifications: Four literal /etc/default/grub settings, fixed supplied normal/recovery templates, bounded virtual menu generation and early-root trace only. No sourcing, expansion, saved defaults, distro discovery/template execution, real grub-mkconfig, bootloader installation, timer waiting, firmware or host file access. Initial ro/rw and quiet presence are modeled; no real remount, console or kernel execution.

initial.instructions: Generate a menu that selects the supplied 7.0 ordinary-startup entry for system UUID 31415926-5358-9793-2384-626433832795. Allow 8 seconds to choose another entry. Keep every supplied normal and recovery path bootable with initial root mode ro; normal entries should receive quiet and recovery entries should not. Test the menu generated from the current settings. Editing or filling settings alone is not a tested configuration.

Both normal and recovery entries must reach the supplied system with initial root mode ro. Put quiet on normal entries only, so recovery can show diagnostic messages. Test the generated menu after your final settings edit; preserve the supplied image and recovery choices.

scenarios.title: Reconnect the BIOS disk to its Linux boot files
scenarios.summary: Diagnose a lost BIOS loader without overwriting another disk or confusing the rescue directory with the installed system.
scenarios.objective: Repair the GRUB BIOS installation on the supplied startup disk /dev/vda using the existing configured boot directory. Reach the Operations system UUID 12345678-9abc-def0-1234-56789abcdef0 with kernel 7.0, initially read-only, and ordinary multi-user startup. Preserve every partition and filesystem, and the archive loader on /dev/vdb. Test the current boot chain after your final repair.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Read the first blocked stage and the supplied disk/directory facts. Repair the intended disk, then Test boot chain again. Reset only this attempt if you overwrote a protected loader.
steps: Inspect the startup disk and mounted directories
Repair the intended loader installation
Verify the full boot chain and preserved archive
scenarios.explanation: BIOS begins at the selected whole disk. GRUB then uses its embedded core and the boot directory chosen during installation. The configured target directory supplies the menu and image/root facts; the rescue environment’s /boot does not. Installation preserves partition and filesystem data in this model and does not generate a menu. A working boot chain still fails the assignment if the archive loader was overwritten.
hints: Use lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS to compare disks and mounted directories. The BIOS startup disk is also shown in Supplied machine.
findmnt -T PATH identifies the filesystem behind a supplied boot directory. cat PATH/grub/grub.cfg reads only its supplied menu.

grub-install takes a whole-disk destination. --boot-directory chooses the mounted directory for GRUB files; it does not choose the firmware startup disk. Test boot chain is a simulator button, not a Linux command.
scenarios.simplifications: Bounded BIOS/MBR i386-pc installation over supplied 512-byte-sector geometry and mounted ext4 directories. Fixed package/core size; symbolic boot records, supplied literal GRUB menu and image/root facts. No actual GRUB, firmware, raw MBR/image bytes, package tools, mount/chroot, BIOS/GPT, EFI, Legacy, blocklists, force or host access. Installation does not generate grub.cfg. Atomic refusal is simulator policy, not real-tool protection.

initial.instructions: Repair the GRUB BIOS installation on the supplied startup disk /dev/vda using the existing configured boot directory. Reach the Operations system UUID 12345678-9abc-def0-1234-56789abcdef0 with kernel 7.0, initially read-only, and ordinary multi-user startup. Preserve every partition and filesystem, and the archive loader on /dev/vdb. Test the current boot chain after your final repair.

example.instructions: Recover the supplied workshop BIOS startup disk /dev/vdc, using its configured boot directory. Preserve the other loader on /dev/vdd; test the resulting boot chain.

scenarios.title: Restore the EFI loader and its boot entry
scenarios.summary: Reconnect a Linux installation to the UEFI boot order while preserving an existing archive startup path.
scenarios.objective: Restore the Operations boot path through the EFI System Partition on /dev/vda1. Use the supplied kernel 7.0 and root UUID 7240d4ce-f757-4103-be48-d903f6e7e9c9 with initially read-only root and ordinary multi-user startup. Preserve Boot0007 and every file on the archive EFI partition. Keep the archive after the intended working entry in BootOrder. Test the current boot chain after your final installation or firmware change.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Inspect the current EFI files, boot entry and BootOrder. Use Test boot chain to see which application started and whether Linux reached the intended root.
steps: Identify the EFI System Partition and the configured boot directory
Install the loader and register its firmware path
Verify the current Linux boot and preserved archive
scenarios.explanation: The EFI System Partition contains the executable. The firmware entry identifies that partition and its loader path. The mounted boot directory contains the GRUB menu and can be on a different disk. The archive stays in BootOrder after the intended working entry.
hints: Use lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS, blkid, and findmnt -T PATH to distinguish the EFI mount from the directory with grub/grub.cfg.
The supplied x86_64-efi installation uses --no-nvram. Register the resulting EFI path separately with efibootmgr.
Use a single-quoted path such as '\EFI\WORKSHOP\GRUBX64.EFI' for the firmware loader argument. Use the partition-relative path, without the Linux mount prefix.
Inspect efibootmgr -v for the actual boot numbers and order. Preserve the archive option and its files.
scenarios.simplifications: Supplied GPT EFI System Partition and bounded FAT32 metadata, symbolic x86_64 loader files, active firmware entries and explicit BootOrder. Linux handoff uses the supplied GRUB menu and early-boot model. Fixed installation package and symbolic boot-directory modules. No host disk, FAT formatting, EFI variables, PE execution, BootNext, removable fallback, Secure Boot, GRUB Legacy or full firmware behavior.

initial.instructions: Restore the Operations boot path through the EFI System Partition on /dev/vda1. Use the supplied kernel 7.0 and root UUID 7240d4ce-f757-4103-be48-d903f6e7e9c9 with initially read-only root and ordinary multi-user startup. Preserve Boot0007 and every file on the archive EFI partition. Keep the archive after the intended working entry in BootOrder. Test the current boot chain after your final installation or firmware change.

example.instructions: Restore the workshop system through /dev/vdc1. Keep Boot0009 and its archive files available after it. Test the resulting boot chain.

scenarios.title: Recover from a removable loader without the internal disk
scenarios.summary: Repair a recovery device whose default loader depends on the internal disk, then verify both startup paths.
scenarios.objective: Repair the x64 default loader on the supplied removable EFI partition /dev/vdb1. With /dev/vda unavailable, reach the Recovery system UUID 7240d4ce-f757-4103-be48-d903f6e7e9c9 with the supplied 7.0 kernel, initially read-only root and rescue.target. Keep ordinary Linux startup through Boot0010. Preserve the original firmware entries, BootOrder and all files outside the removable default loader. Choose Test recovery paths after your final change.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Read the first blocked recovery stage. Check the boot directory and the root UUID in its supplied menu. Test both paths again after the repair.
steps: Inspect the original firmware order and removable EFI path
Diagnose the unavailable boot directory or root
Repair and test both boot paths
scenarios.explanation: The default EFI application starts on the removable device. Its configured boot directory and selected root filesystem must also be available. Keeping the old copied root UUID can break recovery even when the loader and menu are on the removable disk.
hints: Test recovery paths uses normal startup and a second test with the supplied internal disk unavailable.
The x64 removable path is \EFI\BOOT\BOOTX64.EFI. A named loader elsewhere on the partition does not replace that path.
Use findmnt and read the supplied grub/grub.cfg to check both the boot directory and the root UUID. A copied menu may still request the old internal filesystem.
Install with --removable to write the default application path. Preserve the normal firmware order and all other supplied files.
scenarios.simplifications: Explicit x64 removable-media selection, supplied FAT32 ESP and symbolic loader, one unavailable disk and bounded GRUB2 Linux handoff. The missing-disk condition changes observations only. No host disk, mount changes, firmware variables, Secure Boot, live media creation, raw image or actual kernel execution.

initial.instructions: Repair the x64 default loader on the supplied removable EFI partition /dev/vdb1. With /dev/vda unavailable, reach the Recovery system UUID 7240d4ce-f757-4103-be48-d903f6e7e9c9 with the supplied 7.0 kernel, initially read-only root and rescue.target. Keep ordinary Linux startup through Boot0010. Preserve the original firmware entries, BootOrder and all files outside the removable default loader. Choose Test recovery paths after your final change.

example.instructions: Restore the workshop recovery loader on /dev/vdd1. Test with /dev/vdc unavailable and preserve ordinary startup through Boot0024.

scenarios.title: Boot an inspection system once from an edited GRUB entry
scenarios.summary: Correct the inspection entry for a single boot and verify that normal startup stays unchanged.
scenarios.objective: Choose the supplied inspection entry for the 6.14 kernel. Edit its temporary linux line to use the Inspection root and start it read-only. Request rescue.target for this boot. Choose Boot once. Confirm the edited handoff and the later ordinary startup from the saved menu.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Read the edited boot’s blocked stage or unmet requirement. Check the kernel, root UUID and startup request, then boot once again.
steps: Inspect the saved menu and supplied roots
Choose and edit the inspection entry
Compare the edited and ordinary handoffs

lesson.prerequisite_note: Review the disk-preparation unit: read supplied media, count inclusive sectors, distinguish hints from initialized content and preserve existing data. Now plan where partitions go in relation to one another.

concepts.title: Plan for the growing data
concepts.text: Logs record activity and often grow. A preserved archive can divide a disk into several free intervals. Choose a region that holds today’s log partition and leaves the requested space immediately after it.

concepts.title: Adjacent space is different from total space
concepts.text: A raw partition occupies consecutive sectors. To extend its end in place later, the following sectors must be unallocated. A large free interval elsewhere does not remove the next partition blocking its end. This lesson reserves room; it does not perform a resize.

concepts.title: Read the units and count both ends
concepts.text: These virtual disks use 512-byte sectors. One MiB is 1,048,576 bytes, so one MiB contains 2048 sectors. For a chosen size, end = start + size in sectors − 1. The − 1 matters because both endpoints belong to the partition. Starts must be multiples of the supplied 2048-sector alignment.

concepts.title: Keep the growth window unallocated
concepts.text: Do not create a “reserve” partition in the growth window. Even an unformatted partition occupies its sectors. The model counts only unused sectors between your log partition and the next allocation or the GPT metadata at the disk’s end.

concepts.title: Allocate, then initialize content
concepts.text: A Linux data hint describes intended use. It does not create an ext4 filesystem. After adding the partition, select its actual number and initialize ext4 with the required label. Keep the supplied archive and its file intact.

concepts.title: Explore safely in the separate example
concepts.text: Fill selected step changes draft fields only. Add and Initialize change the virtual disk; Check current disk configuration evaluates it. This preparation model cannot delete, resize or overwrite allocations. If an experiment consumes needed space, Reset practice and replay the example. The small MiB capacities are examples for calculating space, not real-system sizing advice.

lesson.description: On the separate /dev/vde practice disk, keep archive at 24–32 MiB. Add samplelogs, 6–10 MiB, with actual ext4 label samplelogs and at least 12 MiB unallocated immediately after it. The worked layout uses sectors 65536–77823 inclusive (6 MiB).

worked.explanation: Fill name, inclusive start/end sectors and type hint. Use Add partition using draft, then read its actual allocated number.
Select the actual applied partition number and choose its format/label, then Initialize selected blank partition. A hint alone is not initialized content.

lesson.try_change: After the practice passes, add the supplied scratch partition inside the growth window and check again. Required filesystems can remain correct while headroom and preservation fail. Use Reset practice and replay; do not look for a delete operation.

solution: Use native allocation and initialization controls. The authored reference is one valid plan, not a required operation order, extent or UUID.

scenarios.objective: Preserve /dev/vda1 boot-ref and its /keep.txt, including its extent, content and identity. On /dev/vda or /dev/vdb create exactly one aligned root partition of 16–24 MiB with actual ext4 label root, one logs partition of 12–20 MiB with actual ext4 label logs, and one swap partition of 4–8 MiB with actual swap label swap. Use Linux data hints for root and logs, and a Linux swap hint for swap. Place root and logs on different supplied disks, and leave at least 24 MiB unallocated immediately after logs. Create GPT only on the eligible blank disk and keep all unrequested allocations unchanged; mounting, activation and boot installation are not required.

lesson.prerequisite_note: Review the disk-preparation unit: read supplied media, count inclusive sectors, distinguish hints from initialized content and preserve existing data. Now plan where partitions go in relation to one another.

concepts.title: Choose a role for each future filesystem
concepts.text: The root filesystem / holds the main directory tree; /var holds changing data such as logs, and /home holds users’ files. /boot holds startup files. Swap is paging space rather than an ordinary filesystem. Names here record intended roles; mounting, swap activation and bootloader installation are separate tasks.

concepts.title: Two partitions are not two disks
concepts.text: Separate fixed filesystems already isolate their ordinary file allocations, even on one disk. This team additionally requires root and logs on different supplied disks so their replacement and future unallocated growth pools can be managed independently. This is a placement policy, not a measurement of I/O performance or hardware failure domains.

concepts.title: Leave a useful growth window
concepts.text: A log partition needs the stated unused space immediately after its end. Put another role somewhere else if it would consume that window. Count inclusive sectors and the reserved GPT tail, rather than treating the entire disk as usable.

concepts.title: Preserve the supplied startup reference
concepts.text: The existing boot-ref partition and /keep.txt are provided data. Keep their location, content and identity unchanged. Only the other supplied disk needs a new GPT. These reference files do not establish that a real operating system would boot.

concepts.title: Check actual signatures and labels
concepts.text: Root and logs need actual ext4 content; swap needs an actual swap signature. Partition hints, names and draft fields alone are incomplete. Any valid unique UUID and any placement/order meeting the required sizes, alignment, disk separation and growth window can work.

concepts.title: Plan before applying an allocation
concepts.text: Add commits a virtual allocation, and this bounded preparation model has no delete or resize. In the separate example, a scratch partition demonstrates a bad growth window; Reset practice and replay to recover. The independent assignment remains your own draft and applied state.

Put sample-root and sample-logs on different disks; leave at least 16 MiB unused immediately after sample-logs.
